meta.title: Twelve More Grips You Already Knew
meta.summary: Every C minor grip on one page, the rule that builds any of them run backwards to read one instead, and a shortcut for naming a bare three-string barre on sight.

spans.text: Twelve grips, and you have already built every one of them, one string set at a time. This page's only job is to put them side by side, and to show that the rule which builds a grip also reads one back.
All twelve, in one table

One idea does all twelve at once, and it runs both directions. Name the inversion, and that tells you which voice is the third: root position, the middle note; first inversion, the bass; second inversion, the top. Drop that voice a fret and you're in minor; raise it a fret and you're back in major. Nothing else in the grip moves. That's the whole reason this chapter needed no new shapes — twelve grips you already had, plus one rule about where the third hides.

Run the rule along a whole neck rather than at one fret, and a set can surprise you about where its cycle starts. On strings 1-2-3, C major's ladder opens at the nut with second inversion. C minor's ladder has no second inversion there at all: it opens on root position, up at fret 3, and the second inversion doesn't arrive until frets 11 to 13 — three bands where major drew four, because the grip that used to sit at the nut had nowhere to go but up.

props.caption: C minor's inversions on strings 1-2-3 — root position opens the set, not second inversion.

spans.text: The cycle's order round the set — root, first, second — is exactly what major's is; only where it starts on the neck has moved. That's the relocation from earlier in the chapter, seen along the whole fretboard instead of at a single fret.
Strings 2-3-4 make the calmer case, because nothing there relocated.

props.caption: C minor's inversions on strings 2-3-4 — same order and starting inversion as major's.

spans.text: First inversion opens at the nut, same as major's; second inversion follows, then root position further up, then first inversion again as the set repeats. Two ladders, one contrast: one set's cycle moved house, the other's didn't budge. Both are silent, same as every ladder before them — no play button, just the shape of the climb.
Reading a grip instead of building one

There's a shortcut hiding in one of these shapes. Every minor first inversion on strings 1-2-3 is flush — all three notes at a single fret. That means a small three-string barre anywhere up there is always
some
minor chord with its third in the bass, and you can name it just by reading the fret.
x x x 0 0 0
is the top three open strings,
G3 B3 E4
— that's
Em
x x x 5 5 5
is
Am
x x x 8 8 8
is
Cm
. Verified for all twelve roots — but it's a claim about this one set only. The flush shape doesn't repeat on 2-3-4, 3-4-5, or 4-5-6, so don't reach for the same trick there.
Any of these twelve will sit alongside every other way to play the same chord in
Chord Shapes
— a useful check that the grip under your fingers is the chord you think it is.

The third has done the whole chapter's work — one note, dropped a fret, twelve times over. What's left still standing is the fifth. Chapter 4 moves that one instead, into the diminished and augmented triads, and that's next.
